AIRFRAME AND ENGINE EXAMINATION
CASE-ANON-001
Accident Date: March 24, 2019
Exam Date: March 27, 2019

A. ACCIDENT
Location: Location-1, Region-West
Date: March 24, 2019
Aircraft: Cessna 172M, N-XXXX, Serial # 1726139
NTSB IIC: Investigator-1

B. EXAMINATION PARTICIPANTS:
Investigator-1  (NTSB, Location-10)
Investigator-3  (Lycoming Engines, Location-12)
Investigator-2  (Textron Aviation, Location-11)

C. SUMMARY
The wreckage was removed from the mountainside and transported to Facility-1 in
Location-8, Region-West on March 26, 2019. Detailed examination of the airframe and engine was conducted
by the NTSB and parties on March 27, 2019 at Facility-1. No evidence of preimpact
mechanical malfunction, or any pre-or post-impact fire was noted during the examination.

D. AIRFRAME EXAMINATION

1.0 General
On-scene information and overall damage patterns were consistent with the airplane
impacting a very steep (approx. 70 degrees from the horizontal) terrain in an upright,
approximately wings- and pitch- level attitude.
All primary components were located at the impact site.

2.0 Fuselage
The cockpit/cabin area was severely disrupted due to crushing and tearing.
The engine was pushed aft into the cabin.
The cabin floor, starting at the firewall, was crushed aft to the main gear attach points.

3.0 Wings
The outboard 3 ft of the left wing leading edge was crushed diagonally aft.
Both fuel caps remained securely fastened in their respective filler necks.

4.0 Flight Controls
All flight controls were present and attached to their respective aerodynamic surfaces.
Control cable continuity was established for the ailerons, elevators, pitch trim, and rudder.
The pitch trim actuator was found in a position corresponding to tab 5 degrees TEU.
The flaps were fully retracted; the flap position indicator registered 40 degrees (full down).

5.0 Controls and Instruments
The tachometer registered 6967.2 hours, and the needle pointed to about 1,600 rpm.
The altimeter Kollsman window was set to 29.82.
The attitude indicator was laid over to the right (left wing down attitude).
Fuel selector set to the right tank.
ELT: ACK Technologies model E-01, serial number 033768 - armed but had not activated.
Battery due date was 12/31/24.
A flight school document found in the airplane indicated tachometer registered 6966 hrs when
the airplane was released to the pilot.
F. ENGINE EXAMINATION

1.0 General
The powerplant was a Lycoming O-320 E2D series engine; four cylinder; air cooled, direct
drive, horizontally opposed, normally aspirated (carburetor), rated at 150hp @ 2700rpm.
Serial # L-44359-27A
Most recent overhaul 9/13/18 (264.8 hours since overhaul)
Most recent annual 11/2/18
Visual examination of the engine revealed no evidence of pre-impact catastrophic mechanical malfunction or fire.

2.0 Engine Internal and Drive Train
The crankshaft and attached connecting rods were free of heat distress.
The camshaft was intact and each of the cam lobes exhibited its characteristic elliptical shape.
There was no evidence of lubrication deprivation.
No signatures or conditions observed consistent with any pre-impact catastrophic mechanical malfunction.

3.0 Fuel System
The fuel system utilizes gravity fed fuel; there is no engine driven fuel pump.
The carburetor was fracture-separated from the engine.
The foam filter element remained securely attached to the airbox bracket; no pre-impact obstruction to airflow.

4.0 Exhaust System
No oil residue observed in the exhaust system gas path.
Maintenance records indicate the muffler and heat shroud were replaced at engine overhaul.
Entry dated 10/15/2018 @ Tach 6702.7.

G. PROPELLER EXAMINATION
The metal two bladed fixed pitch propeller was fracture-separated from the crankshaft flange.
The fracture surfaces exhibited signatures consistent with overload due to the absorption of rotational energy.
The propeller blades displayed varying degrees of leading edge gouging, torsional twisting,
chordwise striations across the cambered surface, and trailing edge S bending.
The signatures were consistent with the absorption of rotational forces applied at the
crankshaft at the time of impact.

E. Customers at Airport-Charlie are using self-service pump provided by Fuel-Vendor-1. Each airplane has
unique fuel card provided by Fuel-Vendor-1 which is used during refuelings for payment. Airline-A then
receives an invoice with total sum at the end of the week and pays for the fuel with a check. After each
refueling, pump prints receipt with N-registration, date and time, price and amount of fuel. This receipt
is given to dispatcher at the end of the flight with paper dispatch ticket. Typically airplane is being
refueled after the flight to full tanks as a courtesy to other customers unless we receive information from
pilots that they do not want full tanks for performance or W&B reasons. If customers are late or not able
to refuel after their flight, they should write remaining fuel on the paper dispatch ticket.

Each airplane has its dipstick available in the airplane to crosscheck the readings with onboard fuel
indicators. If there is a need to refuel, customers taxi the airplane to self service refueling station and

Garmin Aera 660 is a battery-powered portable multi-function display and GPS receiver

port. An internal button-battery is used to provide back-up power to the internal memory

Airline-A Corona base Operational Procedures
Dear pilots,
we would like to welcome you at our Airport-Charlie base. We would like to familiarize you with our
base and company's recommendations and operational procedures for safety of your flights in
California and the surrounding states.

Airline-A is located at Airport-Charlie, east of the city of Los Angeles.
Surrounded by controlled tower airports such as Chino, Riverside, Ontario, etc.

Airport-Charlie is a great place to start your flight training or do your time-building.
The training area is within 15 NM radius from the base, so you do not have to fly far away to
practice maneuvers, instrument approaches, and takeoffs or landings.

Airport-Charlie has 3200 X 60 feet runway lengths and 24 hours self serve fuel service.

Please take a look on following tips to ensure smooth operations:
1. Airport-Charlie is a small and non-towered airport, always watch around prior starting
engine, taxiing and prior entering runway. There might be people operating without using
a radio.
Always announce your intentions on Airport-Charlie traffic at 122.7 Mhz.
2. Taxi slowly, there are multiple airplanes around you and sometimes even people walking
around them.
3. Do not do any runup at parking spot, there are airplanes around and behind you.
4. Prior any flight contact a weather briefer at +1 (800) 992-7433.

5. For after hours briefing or flights use briefing room, ramp entrance code is [REDACTED].
Make sure you lock the room after use.
6. Airport gate is closed for entrance from every day. The gate will open
automatically for you to exit the airport after closing hours.
7. Shall you need oil, ask dispatcher for a full bottle. If you need oil at other locations check
with local FBO's or fuel providers. Oil type used by specific airplane is printed on the
dispatch. Do not mix oil types.
8. After sampling the fuel before flight at Airport-Charlie, if the fuel sample does not have any
contamination return it to the tank. If there is a contamination throw the sample into the
provided bucket and contact dispatcher / mechanic. Please do not spill fuel on the
ground, it damages the tarmac surface.
9. Stay away from LAX Class-B airspace. First time you need to fly with CFI and receive a
checkout from school to go to class B. It is extremely busy and complicated airspace.
10. Bear in mind that Catalina island KAVX and Airport-Echo are NO-GO airports for solo
flights, only specially approved and checked pilots can fly there with our airplanes. Talk
to your instructor about checkout procedures.
11. Anytime you plan to fly over the water you need to have a life jacket onboard for each
pilot and passenger, life jackets must be placed in seat pockets so they are available
during the flight. Do not put them in baggage area. Shall you need them ask dispatcher
for a life jacket before the flight.
12. Do not plan flights with legs longer than 4 hrs for C172 and 3 hrs for C152 (HOBBS)
latest by this time you must land, have a rest, check fuel remaining and oil.
13. All airplanes are equipped with GPS use it smartly to plan your flight.
14. You need to carry a paper version of Sectional chart for any flight or have an ipad with
Foreflight and downloaded pdf with official FAA version of the sectional chart.
15. Do not play with ELT remote switch, if it happens to you to accidentally activate an ELT
during the flight or on the ground, please contact nearest towered airport tower and
announce it to them or call school dispatcher.
16. If there is any technical problem or observation with the airplane contact school
dispatcher for assistance, where possible take a picture or video of the problem and
send it to dispatcher.
17. In summer months weather in California could be extremely hot, make sure that you
have water with you for the flight. Make sure that you calculate density altitude. If you
see large forest fire, do not fly through the smoke it is not safe.
18. Do not fly over open desert areas, they are complicated for VFR navigation, where
possible stick to the highway or railroad.

C. SUMMARY
On March 24, 2019, about 1815 Pacific Standard time, a Cessna 172M airplane, N-XXXX,
impacted mountainous terrain near Location-1, Region-West while on a cross-country flight
to Airport-Bravo, Location-3, Region-West. The commercial pilot and his non pilot-
rated passenger received fatal injuries, and the airplane was destroyed. The airplane was
registered to Airline-A, and was being operated as a 14 Code of
Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. Undetermined night meteorological conditions
existed at the impact location at the time of the accident. The accident flight leg had originated
from Airport-Alpha, Location-2, Region-West.
No evidence consistent with in-flight fire or in-flight structural failure was observed.
D. RESPONSE and SITE LOCATION INFORMATION
1.0 Background and Response
The pilot was conducting a VFR flight to Airport-Bravo from the LA Basin
He was using FAA flight following services and had been assigned a discrete beacon code
The FAA controller was in voice communications with the pilot, and was receiving the
secondary radar returns from the airplane
The pilot advised the controller that he planned to follow a road and remain at an altitude of
3,500 ft (msl) for the entire flight

Voice communications and radar returns from the airplane were lost about 1815
An FAA ALNOT was issued at 1843
Riverside Sheriffs Department personnel located the wreckage in the evening of March 24
Their initial assessment was that the pilot, believed to be the sole person on board, was
fatally injured
FAA inspectors from Riverside FSDO arrived in the morning of March 25
NTSB IIC arrived the afternoon of March 25
The Textron Aviation representative arrived the morning of March 26
2.0 Location, Site Condition, and Ground Scar Information
The accident site coordinates were 34.02574 N, -116.58775 W
The accident site elevation was about 2,465 ft, above and west of the road that the pilot was
believed to be following
The wreckage was about 800 ft west of the north-south road, which was a paved 4-lane
highway (CA Rte 62) that was situated in the river/wash valley that formed a pass through a
small mountain range
The wreckage was on steep, unstable terrain about 300 ft above the road
The wreckage was observed to be precariously situated on the mountain slope, which limited
the extent of the examination of the wreckage in situ
Only a very few items (lower cowl, windscreen fragments, left and right navigation light lens
fragments, right-side cabin door, and one MLG tire) were separated from the main wreckage
o  The lower cowl and the nav light lens fragments were found about 30 ft above the
main wreckage; this is considered to be the impact point
o  The terrain at the impact point and between that and the wreckage was steeper than
the terrain where the wreckage came to rest
o  The observed ground scars (disturbed soil and rocks) were consistent with the airplane
then falling/sliding down to its final resting location
o  The relative locations of the left and right lens fragments were congruent with the
airplane being upright when it struck the mountain face
The forward section of the airplane was upright, and partially covered with soil/rocks that
had slid downhill
The fuselage was severely crushed and torn, and the wings and empennage were severely
torn and deformed
The approximate orientation of the wreckage was on a heading of approximately 230 degrees True
o  The mountain impact face and wreckage distribution were consistent with this also
being the approximate ground track at the time of impact
There was no indication of fire, either inflight or post impact
First responders reported that the airplane was "covered in fuel" when they arrived at the
wreckage (about 0050 March 25)

E. WRECKAGE INFORMATION
1.0 In-Situ Examination
The engine and propeller were nearly completely obscured by the wreckage and/or terrain
debris that slid downhill onto the wreckage
The engine appeared to be upright
The cabin was crushed, torn and deformed, and unrecognizable except by its location
The MLG carry-through structure, including the two MLG legs, was inverted and translated
up and forward from its normal location
The aft fuselage was folded over, up, and forward of its normal position; it was also rotated
about 90 degrees (top surface to airplane left) about its longitudinal axis
The horizontal stabilizer was mostly intact, but mostly separated from the aft fuselage
Both elevators remained attached to the horizontal stabilizer, and the pitch trim tab remained
attached to the right elevator
The fin remained attached to the aft fuselage, and the rudder remained attached to the fin
Both wings were upright, but crushed, torn, and swept aft about 45 degrees
Both wings had LE aft crushing continuously across their full spans
Both ailerons remained attached to the wings
Both flaps remained attached to their wings, and appeared to be fully retracted
Both fuel caps were observed installed securely in their respective filler necks
All flight control surface balance weights appeared to be present
Multiple control cables were visible, but their routing and continuity could not be determined
due to the level of damage
Only a portion of one individual, a male, was able to be seen at first; the total number of
occupants was initially unable to be determined, due to the condition of the wreckage
Some personal items and luggage was able to be accessed from the wreckage while it was on
the hillside
o  The items included the reported pilot's wallet with his pilot and medical certificates
o  A small piece of hand luggage appeared to belong to a female, and when it was
opened, it contained female clothing and accessories
The luggage indications prompted further attempts to locate additional victims in the
wreckage, and another person (likely female) was detected
2.0 Post-Hillside Recovery
The condition and location of the wreckage warranted its extraction by helicopter
The helicopter crew packaged and recovered the wreckage to a clearing about a mile from
the accident site
The two (and only) victims were recovered from the wreckage
The wreckage was partially examined and photographed and loaded onto a truck for transport
to a secure facility where it could be examined in detail
The all metal fixed pitch two blade propeller was fracture-separated from the engine at its
attach flange

The onboard clock was stopped at 0115:47 (consistent with being set to UTC time,
equivalent to 1815:47 PST)
The artificial horizon was fracture-separated from the instrument panel
o  It was date stamped January 2, 2019
No other useful instrument or control indications were able to be made at this time

Commercial Pilot, to rent a C172 at Airline-A in Location-4 for the purpose of
time-building in the Southern California area on February 28th, 2019.

The first hour and a half I spent with Pilot-1 we did Ground School going over everything
listed in the FAA's Conducting an Effective Flight Review guide. We covered all the topics in
the regulatory review guide discussing PAVE (Pilot / Aircraft / EnVironment / External
Pressures). I was overall impressed with his level of Aeronautical Knowledge and focus on
safety. Of all the Country-A time-building students I personally checked out at Airline-A in

Since Pilot-1 did all of his flight training in Location-15, Region-Southeast I focused heavily on how to navigate and

towards Victorville through the Cajon Pass and East towards Location-5 through the Banning
Pass. I warned him about both of these mountain passes, Cajon and Banning, that the winds
can become very strong as the two mountain ranges will both form a wind funnel. We did not
discuss any flight plan into Location-3 - his destination at the time of the accident. He flew his
own way to Location-3 and back several times after my Checkout before his accident. I was not
at the airport and had no knowledge of him renting the plane to fly to Location-3 the day of his

Lake Matthews Practice Area where I had him perform Commercial Maneuvers, Stalls, and all of
